name: Lena Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior operator on the bottling line at Marlow Dairy, the one that fills milk and cream into plastic bottles. I get in at 5:30, check the filler heads, the capper and the label machine, and then I keep an eye on the line for eight hours. If one filler head drifts by a few millilitres, I hear about it from quality, so I check by hand more often than the manual says.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a line that runs smooth for a whole shift, no stops and no spills. What wears me out is the cold in the filling hall, standing on wet floors, and the changeovers, when we switch from milk to cream and have to wash everything down. My knees tell me every evening that I'm 58.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing new. We've heard all this before with the barcode scanners and with the touch screens, and the line still needs me. I'd tell my crew not to get excited either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not really bothered about AI, but I'm bothered about the dairy. Two supermarkets buy most of what we make, and if one of them switches suppliers, we lose a shift. I'm 58 with four years to go, and I don't want to be hunting for a job at 59.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I do, stay on the line, work the same shifts and not change a thing. I'd keep my head down and put away what I can, maybe 100 a month. And I'd say yes to whatever overtime comes up, because I'd rather have the money in the bank than be asked later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, I suppose. A bit flat, but flat is fine at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the plant has its own pressures. What are they right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supermarkets keep squeezing the price, and the plant squeezes us. Last winter they cut the Saturday shift and brought it back after three months. My husband Imran works at the council depot, which is steady, but we have only about three months of savings if something goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with computers at work today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very little. I punch in on a screen and I look at the line dashboard, and I do the temperature log on a tablet. I don't like the tablet, I'd rather use paper, and I've never used any of the chatbots people talk about.

say: I'd say **nothing new** here, since we heard the same about barcode scanners and touch screens.
I'd tell my crew not to get **excited** either way.
think: I'm not bothered about AI, but I'm bothered about the **dairy** and its two big supermarket buyers.
I'm 58 with **four years** to go and don't want to hunt for a job at 59.
do: Stay on the **bottling line** and work the same shifts without changing anything.
Put away about **100 a month** in extra savings.
Say yes to **overtime** when it comes up.
feel: **Flat**, but flat is fine at my age.
S0.quote: I'm not really bothered about AI
fieldNote: **The dairy's finances** worry her more than AI does, and the Saturday shift cut last winter shows why.
**Low tech comfort**: she prefers paper to a tablet and has never used a chatbot.
**Savings** are about three months, so she takes overtime rather than risk gaps.

steps.text: Stay on the bottling line and keep the same shifts
Put an extra 100 a month into savings
Say yes to every overtime shift offered
Wait to see if the supermarkets change suppliers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be messy. The office people will go first, the ones who do orders and invoices, and the line gets more screens. I'd tell my crew to not volunteer for anything they don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be nervous. If the ordering and scheduling go to software, there'll be fewer supervisors, and a senior operator like me is in the same pay band. I don't trust a plant to keep the older, higher-paid people when a cheaper way appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put and keep my head down, and I'd keep the best attendance record on the line. I'd cut back on our extras, like the weekend takeaways and the streaming, and aim for five months of savings. If they asked me to train on the new control screens, I'd go, even if I grumble about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. I feel I'm being asked to learn something I don't want to, just to keep what I already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dashboard work is a bit of thinking work. Does any of that change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. The production plan on the screen already shows up pre-made, and I tick it off. If software tells the line what to run, nobody needs me to understand why, only to push the button, and then I'm easier to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the plant offered you a different role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no thank you, probably. I like my line, my crew and my shift. If it was between that and no job, I'd take it, but I'd be sulking all the way there.

say: I'd say it will be **messy**: office people go first and the line gets more screens.
I'd tell my crew not to volunteer for things they don't **understand**.
think: With fewer supervisors, a **senior operator** in the same pay band looks expensive.
I don't trust a plant to keep **older, higher-paid** people when a cheaper way appears.
do: Stay put and keep the best **attendance record** on the line.
Cut weekend takeaways and streaming to reach **five months** of savings.
Go on training for the new **control screens**, even if I grumble.
feel: **Uncomfortable**, as if I'm being asked to learn something I don't want just to keep what I have.
fieldNote: **Cost worry**: she fears that being senior and well paid makes her easy to replace.
**Resistance** is real but she'd still take training if it saved her job.
**Little control**: she expects to react rather than plan.

steps.text: Keep the best attendance record on the line
Cut weekend takeaways and the streaming subscription
Save up to five months of household bills
Go on the plant's training for the new control screens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody needs to tell us the truth, because two years is nothing and the government is always last to speak. At the plant I'd ask the manager straight out what his plan is. He'd say he doesn't know, and that would tell me what I needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be terrified, to be honest. Even if robots only come in 2031, the plant will start rebuilding long before, and the older people are the first to be offered a package. I'm not a person who has a plan B, and I don't have the money to build one in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Imran and sit down with the numbers the same night. I'd cut everything we could, aim for six months in the bank, and ask the plant what the early-leaver terms are. I'd look at the council's retraining courses, but I'd be doing it with no real hope, since I've never been a student.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awful. I'd be lying awake and listening to the fridge hum, doing the same sums again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about 2031. Do you think of that as safe time for your hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to think so, but I don't trust it. The planning and ordering go in 2028, and without those, a dairy might cut half its staff overnight. Three years on, the robots would do the bottling line, and I'd be 63, too old for any new job and too young to draw a full pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Sana that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sana to keep her nursing job and not to worry about her mum. I'd tell her we have the house and each other. And I'd tell her not to move far away, because I'd want her close if things went wrong.

say: I'd say somebody needs to **tell us the truth**, because two years is nothing.
I'd ask the plant manager **straight out** what his plan is.
think: The plant would start **rebuilding** long before 2031, and older people get offered packages first.
I don't have a **plan B** or the money to build one in two years.
do: Sit down with Imran and the **numbers** that same night.
Cut everything possible and aim for **six months** in the bank.
Ask the plant for the **early-leaver terms** and look at council retraining courses.
feel: **Awful**, lying awake listening to the fridge hum and redoing the same sums.
Afraid of being too old for a new job and too young for a **full pension**.
S2.quote: I'm not a person who has a plan B
fieldNote: **Alarmed** because she expects the older, senior people to be the first offered a package.
**No plan B** and little confidence in retraining.
**Family comfort**: her first thought is Sana and keeping her close.

steps.text: Sit down with Imran and work out the household numbers that night
Cut everything non-essential and build six months in the bank
Ask the plant for early-leaver terms in writing
Look at the council's retraining courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's more bearable, but not good. Five years goes by very fast, and the plant won't act until the last minute. I'd tell people on my crew to put some money aside while they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I think is that I might just scrape through. If AI arrives when I'm 63, I'd be at the end of my career, and robots by 66 would be someone else's problem. Still, there's no pension fund big enough to relax, so I'd be watching the dairy's numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work the next five years carefully. I'd save about 200 a month, pay off the car and keep my attendance spotless. I'd also ask Imran to put off his own retirement so we both have an income, since the council gives him a pension at 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the last one, but I'd feel a bit like a person waiting for a train that might not come. It's not panic, just a long low worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you more room. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd have time to save and clear the car loan. I wouldn't need to rush to learn anything, because the thinking AI hits the office first and I'd probably be near my last year by the time the plant gets robots. That's a lot less frightening than the two-year picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your outlook on the dairy change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd start looking at which dairies nearby are modern and which are old, because the old ones close first. If Marlow looked weak, I'd move to a stronger plant, even if I'd hate to leave.

say: I'd say it's more bearable but not good, and the plant won't act until the **last minute**.
I'd tell my crew to **put money aside** while they can.
think: I might just **scrape through**, since AI arrives when I'm 63 and robots at 66.
No pension fund is big enough to relax, so I'd watch the **dairy's numbers**.
do: Save about **200 a month** and pay off the car.
Ask Imran to keep working so we both have an **income**.
Compare nearby dairies and be ready to move to a **stronger plant**.
feel: Like waiting for a train that might not come, a **long, low worry** rather than panic.
S3.quote: Five years goes by very fast
fieldNote: **Anxious but not panicked**: time lets her save, but the dairy's health is still a worry.
**Practical**: she thinks about which plants will survive, not about learning AI.
**Household plan** includes her husband's pension at 65.

steps.text: Save 200 a month and pay off the car loan
Compare nearby dairies and move if Marlow looks weak

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably fine for people my age, and it's for the young ones to sort out. I'd say it with a bit of guilt, because I'm sure it'll be harder for them. Still, ten years is time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much. I'd be 68, retired for years, and the dairy's problems would be somebody else's. I'd just want to know the pension was safe, because the funds are always the first thing politicians promise and the last they protect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working until 62, then retire. I'd take on a part-time job at the garden centre near my house, because I'd get bored. I'd keep the money in plain savings and the pension, and I wouldn't try to learn any new technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, I think. It's the kind of future I don't have to live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you well past retirement. What is left to worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry that the pension scheme could change by then, or that the dairy could close and cut the extras it promised. I'd also worry about the price of things, because if machines make everything, who pays for it, and who buys it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son Zayn, if he's starting out in a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Zayn to learn a trade like electrics or plumbing, something with hands and brains together. Machines will be everywhere, and somebody has to fix them. And I'd tell him to save every month, even when it's small.

say: I'd say it's probably fine for people my age and a puzzle for the **young ones**.
I'd say ten years is **time to build** something.
think: For me nothing much, since I'd be **retired** and the dairy's problems would be someone else's.
I'd only want to know the **pension** is safe.
do: Take a part-time job at the nearby **garden centre** so I'm not bored.
Keep money in plain **savings** and the pension, and skip new technology.
feel: **Calm**, because it's a future I don't have to live in.
S4.quote: I'd tell my son Zayn to learn
fieldNote: **Secure by timing**: with ten years she is likely retired before anything lands.
**Pension anxiety** remains her one lingering concern.
**Advice to the young** is practical: trades with hands and brains.

steps.text: Take a part-time job at the garden centre near home
Tell Zayn to learn electrics or plumbing

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It leaves no time, and I'm the kind of person who needs time. What would help is a fair package for older workers who don't want to be retrained, and a pension that doesn't shrink if the plant lets me go early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what we think of the managers. Most of the managers are decent, but they get told what to do from the head office in another city. If somebody there would come and stand on a wet floor for a day, they'd think differently.

headlineQuote: Most of the managers are decent
portrait: **Lena** is a 58-year-old senior bottling-line operator at a dairy, four years from retirement, and she has never used an AI tool.
She is pragmatic and sceptical, worrying more about the **dairy's contracts** than about technology.
She has about **three months** of savings and a husband with a steady council job and pension.
Her mood climbs to **alarmed** in the two-year picture, because older, well-paid workers are first in line for packages.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because it leaves no time, and she needs time.
whatWouldHelp: A fair **package for older workers** and a pension that doesn't shrink if the plant lets her go early.
